statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether women and men who enter treatment for alcohol or other drug use disorders differ in how long they stay or how well they do: as summarized by two narrative reviews from one research group, most large studies found no gender difference in retention, completion or outcome; where differences appeared, the 2007 review found that they generally favoured women, while most of the differences the 2018 update lists, for quitting smoking and for particular medicines, went against women; the reviews' figures are second-hand. A review of 280 articles published from 1975 to 2005 (11.8% of them randomized trials; the studies were not appraised) describes large multi-programme data sets with very few gender differences in retention (among 10,010 patients in 96 programmes, men were 20% less likely than women to stay 90 days in outpatient drug-free care; in a national study of 4,689 adults, gender was not associated with completion after adjustment), small clinical studies that disagreed (five found women more likely to drop out, two less likely), and outcome studies that mostly found no difference and, where they found one, mostly favoured women (in one study of older adults in outpatient alcohol treatment, 79.3% of women and 54% of men were abstinent at 6 months, a difference that disappeared after adjustment for length of stay, although the women still reported no heavy-drinking days in the past month against an average of four among the men) (Greenfield et al., 2007). The group's 2018 update describes no gender difference in outcome in large randomized trials (COMBINE, 1,226 people with alcohol dependence, 31% women; a prescription-opioid trial, 653 people, 40% women), none in retention across 24 NIDA Clinical Trials Network trials (more than 11,000 people), and none in completion across more than 1.7 million US treatment episodes, except that women less often completed detoxification; behavioural treatments and mutual-help groups showed no clear difference between women and men. The exceptions it lists mostly go against women: worse results in quitting smoking, nicotine replacement working better in men, and worse responses in women to disulfiram for cocaine dependence and to buspirone for cannabis and cocaine dependence (where buspirone did no better than placebo in either sex); one smoking medicine, varenicline, worked better in women in one meta-analysis and gave women more benefit than other aids in another, naltrexone findings for alcohol were mixed, and the effect of disulfiram for alcohol dependence in women is unknown because women were, for example, 1.2% of trial participants (McHugh et al., 2018). Comparisons of women-only with mixed-gender treatment were few and mixed. Of the randomized comparisons described in the 2007 review, one found no difference in early dropout, one found better retention in a women-only day programme, and in the one that compared alcohol and drug outcomes the women-only day programme did not differ from two community mixed-gender programmes and had lower abstinence than a hospital programme that cost twice as much per week; the review, relaying the conclusion of that trial's authors, says that women may be equally well served by good programmes of either kind and that changing a programme to women-only does not by itself change outcomes (Greenfield et al., 2007). The 2018 update describes comparisons in which women in women-only programmes did better (across 43 programmes, despite greater severity; and on later crime and incarceration, designs not described), randomized trials it cites as supporting programmes designed for particular groups of women (women with children, with co-occurring psychiatric disorders or in the criminal justice system), and two trials of the group's own women's group therapy: better than mixed-gender group counselling at 6 months in a small first trial, and as effective, not more, in a larger one (McHugh et al., 2018). These comparisons are between women and men who had already entered treatment; within trials, women and men were compared as subgroups, not assigned at random; outcomes were defined in many different ways; a non-significant difference is not evidence that outcomes are the same; and several of the analyses are the reviewers' own. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Once in treatment, do women do as well as men? Most large studies found no difference: women and men stayed in treatment about as long and had similar results. Where differences did appear, the older review found that women mostly did better, while the newer one listed more results in which women did worse, mainly in quitting smoking and with some medicines. Programmes for women only gave mixed results: in the one trial that compared results, a women-only programme showed no difference from two mixed ones and did less well than a costlier hospital programme, and some other studies favoured women-only programmes. All of this comes from two reviews by one research group, which did not check the quality of the studies, and finding no difference is not proof that results are the same.
population: Women and men who had entered treatment for alcohol or other drug use disorders, mostly in the USA, in studies described by two narrative reviews (1975–2005 and 2007–2017)
exposure: Being a woman (an observed characteristic, not assigned at random, even within trials)
comparator: Men in the same programmes or trials
outcome: Retention, completion and substance use outcomes, as each study defined them
magnitude: Second-hand, none pooled, mostly without intervals. Greenfield et al. (2007): 280 articles 1975–2005, 11.8% randomized trials; small clinical retention studies, five with more dropout in women, two with less, one mixed; 10,010 patients in 96 programmes, men 20% less likely to stay 90 days in outpatient drug-free care; 26,047 patients in 87 Los Angeles programmes, women more often completed where differences appeared; 4,689 adults (1,239 women), gender not associated with completion after adjustment; older adults, abstinence in the past 30 days at 6 months 79.3% of women vs 54% of men, not significant after adjustment for length of stay, heavy-drinking days in the past month none in women vs an average of four in men; randomized comparison of outcomes in women-only against mixed-gender day programmes, women-only no different from two community programmes, lower total abstinence than a hospital programme costing twice as much per week. McHugh et al. (2018): COMBINE (n = 1,226, 31% women) and a prescription-opioid trial (n = 653, 40% women), no gender difference in outcome; 24 Clinical Trials Network trials (n > 11,000), no difference in retention; more than 1.7 million treatment episodes, no difference in completion except detoxification (women less often); smoking cessation worse in women; nicotine replacement better in men; varenicline better in women in one meta-analysis and, in another of 32 trials (n = 14,389, 51% women), comparable against placebo with more benefit for women relative to other aids; disulfiram for cocaine dependence and buspirone for cannabis and cocaine dependence worse in women; naltrexone for alcohol mixed; women 1.2% of participants in the disulfiram trials for alcohol cited as an example; women in women-only programmes better on drug use across 43 programmes (observational).

evidence.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Outcome, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As summarized: nicotine dependence is the exception to the pattern of no gender difference, with worse outcomes in women; nicotine replacement worked better in men in a large randomized study; varenicline worked better in women in one meta-analysis and, in another of 32 trials (14,389 people, 51% women), as well in both sexes against placebo but with greater benefit for women relative to nicotine patch and bupropion; there is some evidence that with naltrexone for smoking, men reduced smoking more and women gained less weight. For other medicines, gender differences were not consistently shown: women responded worse to disulfiram for cocaine dependence; a poorer response in women has not been reported in trials of disulfiram for alcohol dependence, perhaps because women were badly under-represented (for example 1.2%); naltrexone for alcohol dependence gave mixed findings (men better under some dosing; no difference in COMBINE); no significant difference with buprenorphine or methadone; women did worse than men with buspirone for cannabis and for cocaine dependence, where buspirone did not beat placebo in either sex.

risk_of_bias.note: Not appraisable: neither review appraised the studies it describes (cards sc_greenfield_2007: some concerns; sc_mchugh_2018: high); within trials, women and men are compared as subgroups, not by random assignment; several analyses are the reviewers' own.

inconsistency.note: The large studies agree on no difference in retention, completion and overall outcome. The differences found point both ways and differ by era and treatment (programmes and psychosocial treatment in the 2007 review, mostly favouring women where present; quitting smoking and particular medicines in the 2018 update, mostly against women), which the claim states; small clinical studies of retention split five to two against women.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: every anchor is a narrative review's account (METHODS §6.3); people who had entered treatment, mostly in US programmes; outcome definitions vary from 30-day abstinence to completion.

imprecision.note: Intervals are not given for most comparisons, so a non-significant difference cannot be shown to be small (METHODS §6.3, absence of evidence).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from two narrative reviews.

grade.reasoning: The studies described are mostly observational, and even in the trials gender is an observed subgroup, so the evidence starts low; down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision: very low, the floor. Rests only on narrative reviews: stays at draft, its figures are second-hand, and it is not for the at-a-glance box (METHODS §6.3). Counted once: McHugh et al. (2018) updates Greenfield et al. (2007) with the same search terms and authors. Status replicated: as described, several independent large data sets and trials (multi-programme data sets, the Alcohol and Drug Services Study, COMBINE, a prescription-opioid trial, 24 Clinical Trials Network trials, 1.7 million treatment episodes) agree on no difference in retention, completion and overall outcome; the specific differences point both ways and differ by era and treatment, which the claim states rather than summarizing them as favouring women; the relation is insufficient evidence because no difference was shown to be small.
